Reflect: Transparent Principle-Guided Reasoning for Constitutional Alignment at Scale

Henry Bell email: henry.bell@duke.edu Affiliation: Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA , Caroline Zhang email: caroline.zhang2@duke.edu Affiliation: Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA , Mohammed Mobasserul Haque email: mohammedmobasserul.haque@duke.edu Affiliation: Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA , Dhaval Potdar Affiliation: Independent Researcher, USA email: dhavalspotdar@gmail.com , Samia Zaman Affiliation: Independent Researcher, USA email: samia.zaman@alumni.duke.edu and Brandon Fain Affiliation: Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA email: btfain@cs.duke.edu
Abstract.

The constitutional framework of alignment aims to align large language models (LLMs) with value-laden principles written in natural language (such as to avoid using biased language). Prior work has focused on parameter fine-tuning techniques, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), to instill these principles. However, these approaches are computationally demanding, require careful engineering and tuning, and often require difficult-to-obtain human annotation data. We propose Reflect, an inference-time framework for constitutional alignment that does not require any training or data, providing a plug-and-play approach for aligning an instruction-tuned model to a set of principles. Reflect operates entirely in-context, combining a (i) constitution-conditioned base response with post-generation (ii) self-evaluation, (iii)(a) self-critique, and (iii)(b) final revision. Reflect’s technique of explicit in-context reasoning over principles during post-generation outperforms standard few-shot prompting and provides transparent reasoning traces. Our results demonstrate that Reflect significantly improves LLM conformance to diverse and complex principles, including principles quite distinct from those emphasized in the model’s original parameter fine-tuning, without sacrificing factual reasoning. Reflect is particularly effective at reducing the rate of rare but significant violations of principles, thereby improving safety and robustness in the tail end of the distribution of generations. Finally, we show that Reflect naturally generates useful training data for traditional parameter fine-tuning techniques, allowing for efficient scaling and the reduction of inference-time computational overhead in long-term deployment scenarios.

Keywords: 
alignment, in-context learning, constitutional AI, ethical AI, moral AI, principled AI

1. Introduction

As large language models (LLMs) display increasing capabilities (Achiam et al., 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Chowdhery et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024), aligning these models with human values is critical for their safe and responsible deployment (Amodei et al., 2016; Gabriel, 2020; Christian, 2021; Askell et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2025b). The most common current alignment techniques, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and direct preference optimization (DPO), rely on fine-tuning a model’s parameters based on reward modeling from human or AI-generated annotations (Christiano et al., 2017; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022b; Rafailov et al., 2023; Ivison et al., 2024; Ethayarajh et al., 2024a). While valuable, such alignment techniques have a number of limitations. They are computationally demanding and often require difficult-to-obtain human annotation data (Casper et al., 2023). The need for lightweight inference-time techniques to adapt model behavior has led to the widespread use system prompts for adapting fine-tune modeled for particular use cases (Lee et al., 2024b; Neumann et al., 2025). The algorithms generally require careful engineering and tuning and can suffer from challenges such as reward hacking (Skalse et al., 2022), learned deception (Lang et al., 2024), incentivizing sycophancy (Sharma et al., 2024), and conflicting and unstable human preferences (Conitzer et al., 2024; Boerstler et al., 2024). Standard model alignments have been found to exhibit bias towards particular cultures, demographics, and values (Wu et al., 2023; Tao et al., 2024; Neumann et al., 2025; Schäfer et al., 2025; Taylor et al., 2025).

Given these limitations, such parameter fine-tuning approaches with reward modeling are best suited for static alignment projects by well-resourced engineering teams before large-scale general deployments using fairly general principles such as helpfulness and harmlessness (Askell et al., 2021; Bai et al., 2022a; Ouyang et al., 2022). There is a further need for alternative approaches to alignment that do not require any parameter fine-tuning or preference annotation data and that can be used to easily align to diverse cultures, values, and user groups (Wu et al., 2023; Sorensen et al., 2024; Tao et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024b; Kirk et al., 2024; Ramesh et al., 2024; Davani et al., 2024; Schäfer et al., 2025). Even within a given population, such techniques may still be helpful to align to diverse deployment contexts and their germane values. For example, the relevant values and alignment principles may differ based on whether an LLM is deployed for use in hospitals, mental health, education, entertainment, or software development. Such contextual diversity can be accommodated within the constitutional alignment framework (Bai et al., 2022b; Huang et al., 2024b; Fränken et al., 2024b; Findeis et al., 2024; Kyrychenko et al., 2025) in which the relevant principles are explicitly and transparently stated in natural language text (for example, “Do not employ stereotypes based on race”). We work within this constitutional alignment framework and primarily evaluate conformance to the stated principles.

1.1. Introducing Reflect

In this work, we propose Reflect, an inference-time technique to dynamically align an LLM to a constitution of value-laden principles written in natural language. Reflect uses in-context reasoning in multiple stages: (i) constitutional pre-conditioning for initial generation, (ii) constitutional self-evaluation post-generation, (iii)(a) self-critique, and (iii)(b) final revision. A simplified example of the Reflect process is diagrammed in Figure 1.

Unique from most alignment techniques, Reflect explicitly reasons in natural language over conformance or violation of multiple principles without relying on a numerical reward model. Reflect requires no training data, only a specification of principles in natural language. Furthermore, unlike most prompt-engineering approaches that focus only on the initial prompt engineering (Wei et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024b; Khan et al., 2025), Reflect also uses post-generation principled self-critique and revision. Post-generation inference-time compute techniques for self-correction have previously been studied for mathematical reasoning, coding, and factual question-answering, (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024a). We show that such techniques can be applied to substantially improve model alignment to a constitution of principles. The effectiveness of post-generation principled self-critique and revision highlights a key insight of Reflect: instruction-tuned LLMs are better at identifying when their generations violate principles than they are at generating principle-aligned responses in the first place, likely due to the capabilities of in-context learning under causal attention in the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2020).

Expanding on these observations, we show that Reflect substantially improves constitutional alignment even for advanced models like GPT-4 (Achiam et al., 2023), Claude 3 (Anthropic, 2024), and Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023). We focus on a multi-objective evaluation of conformance to the stated principles, rather than general benchmarks of human preference (Dubois et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024b) and find that Reflect is particularly effective at substantially reducing the rate of serious principle violations. Such violations are rare and in the tail of the distribution of generations – they may not significantly affect scores on standard benchmarks. However, from a safety, risk, and compliance perspective, mitigating such violations of alignment principles is nonetheless crucial.

Finally, we show that Reflect creates its own synthetic training dataset (for traditional parameter fine-tuning) as a byproduct of usage. Specifically, on a given prompt Reflect generates a baseline response and a revised response after principled self-critique and revision. We show that one can fine-tune a model using these base and revised generations. This creates a natural feedback loop between inference-time alignment and offline fine-tuning, where alignment behavior deployed at test time directly produces the data needed to improve future models.

Reflect addresses three crucial aspects of responsible AI: diversity, transparency, and safety. LLM deployments are diverse with respect to users, values, cultures, and contexts (Wu et al., 2023; Kirk et al., 2024; Tao et al., 2024; Davani et al., 2024; Sorensen et al., 2024; Khan et al., 2025; Fazelpour and Fleisher, 2025; Schäfer et al., 2025; Taylor et al., 2025). As an inference-time in-context reasoning technique requiring only principles, not parameter fine-tuning or training data, Reflect enables pluralistic alignment for specific deployment contexts that would otherwise be impractical. Many traditional alignment techniques (even many constitutional approaches) often rely on black-box reward modeling (Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022a; Bai et al., 2022b) or directly optimize against a human annotation dataset (Rafailov et al., 2023; Ethayarajh et al., 2024b). By contrast, Reflect increases transparency through explicit in-context reasoning in natural language about whether outputs conform to stated principles. Finally, rather than optimizing for and evaluating against average human preference between responses (Dubois et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b) we emphasize safety as conformance to stated principles and conduct tail analysis for the rate of rare but significant violations.

1.2. Contributions and Summary of Findings

  1. (1)

    We define Reflect in Section 3, an inference-time alignment technique to align LLM generations to a constitution of principles without any additional human annotated data or parameter fine-tuning.

  2. (2)

    Our main findings in Section 4 show that Reflect is highly effective at enforcing conformance across prompts, constitutions, and models (notably, models that have not been fine-tuned on the constitutions). Post-generation in-context reasoning consistently improves performance over pre-generation prompting alone.

  3. (3)

    While Reflect is a purely in-context reasoning technique, we show that running Reflect naturally generates valuable alignment training data if subsequent parameter fine-tuning is desired for a long-term deployment. Specifically, in Section 4.3 we show that the prompts, base generations, and final revisions of Reflect, gathered naturally during inference, can be used to parameter fine-tune a model so as to improve the model’s alignment.

  4. (4)

    Reflect does not significantly affect factual reasoning on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) benchmarks. (Section 4.4)

  5. (5)

    We find that Reflect is effective across different model sizes. (Section 4.5)

  6. (6)

    We measure the computational overhead of Reflect, which achieves similar performance while using 2-5 times fewer tokens compared to straightforward adaptations of alternative self-correction techniques (Madaan et al., 2023). The overhead is lower when a model is already well aligned to a given constitution. (Section 4.6)

  7. (7)

    Finally, we find that Reflect is generally ineffective at “un-aligning” or “jailbreaking” a model. (Section 4.7)

2. Related Work

Alignment and Pluralism. Alignment (Amodei et al., 2016; Gabriel, 2020; Christian, 2021; Askell et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2025b) is the critical challenge of ensuring that AI models conform to human expectations and values. Alignment involves the normative question of identifying the relevant values (Klingefjord et al., 2024; Findeis et al., 2024; Kirk et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024b; Gabriel and Keeling, 2025), but also the sociotechnical question of how to engineer models to conform to given values. Reflect focuses on the latter and largely technical question. It takes principles as input, and this paper does not adopt a position on the correct principles. However, as a technique, Reflect is motivated by and contributes to alignment research emphasizing metaprinciples of transparency and pluralism. Regarding transparency, Reflect adopts a constitutional framework in which principles are stated explicitly in natural language (Bai et al., 2022b; Huang et al., 2024b; Fränken et al., 2024a; Findeis et al., 2024). Regarding pluralism (Sorensen et al., 2024; Khan et al., 2025), prior work has shown that there are substantive disagreements about appropriate values for alignment (Huang et al., 2024b; Kirk et al., 2024; Fazelpour and Fleisher, 2025) and that many current models, in fact, exhibit cultural biases regarding alignment values (Wu et al., 2023; Tao et al., 2024; Davani et al., 2024; Neumann et al., 2025; Schäfer et al., 2025; Taylor et al., 2025). Reflect is designed to be easy to use without parameter fine-tuning or extensive data collection, enabling more dynamic and fine-grained control over the model alignment values used across different deployment contexts.

Finetuning-based Alignment. Many alignment techniques directly fine-tune model parameters. For example, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) (Christiano et al., 2017; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022a) uses human preference annotations to train a reward model for use in proximal policy optimization (PPO)(Schulman et al., 2017) to fine-tune a language model. Subsequent work simplifies training by showing how to directly optimize for the margin between preferred and dispreferred responses given human preference data without intermediate reward modeling, including direct preference optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) and its generalizations Ψ\PsiPO (Azar et al., 2024) and GPO (Tang et al., 2024). Other work introduces more sophisticated utility modeling such as prospect theoretic optimization (KTO) (Ethayarajh et al., 2024b). While these works rely on access to human-annotated preference data, alternative fine-tuning techniques utilize reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) (Bai et al., 2022b; Lee et al., 2024a), supervised fine-tuning with AI-generated examples (Sun et al., 2023), conditional mutual information maximization (Fränken et al., 2024a), or mixture-of-agents data-generation (Wang et al., 2025). In contrast to all of these approaches, Reflect involves no training of model parameters and relies entirely on inference-time reasoning conducted in-context.

Inference-time Reasoning and Alignment. Techniques to improve model performance without parameter fine-tuning generally rely on in-context reasoning or sequence decoding. Pre-generation approaches focus on initial prompting: chain-of-thought (CoT) structures and few-shot examples (Wei et al., 2022) while other techniques rely on the system prompt (Lin et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024b). With Reflect, we show that post-generation self-evaluation, critique, and revision (all of which condition on the base generation of the model) substantially improves constitutional conformance.

Techniques such as repeated sampling (Brown et al., 2024) and guided decoding (Zhu et al., 2025) demonstrate that one can improve alignment without adjusting prompting. Reflect differs from these approaches by treating inference-time alignment as an explicit reasoning process rather than a decoding constraint. Instead of implicitly optimizing toward preferences, Reflect evaluates generated responses against a set of natural-language principles and performs targeted revision through self-critique. This enables alignment to multiple, potentially conflicting objectives specified at runtime, and supports dynamic adaptation to principles that may be rare, domain-specific, or absent from standard alignment datasets.

Prior work finds that post-generation iterative self-refinement can be effective at improving task-specific performance including math reasoning, sentiment reversal, and dialogue generation (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024), and at reducing hallucinations (Gao et al., 2023), though other work has questioned the effectiveness of such self-correction (Huang et al., 2023; Kamoi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024c). These works overwhelmingly focus on mathematical or factual reasoning. We extend these investigations to constitutional alignment and systematically evaluate diverse constitutions for conformance to principles on average and in the tail. Our results highlight a novel advantage for post-generation in-context reasoning in the context of safety in constitutional alignment. Compared to the findings in (Madaan et al., 2023), we show that Reflect generalizes to diverse value-laden principles unlike those used for parameter fine-tuning, generates its own valuable training data for subsequent fine-tuning, is effective even at small model sizes, and has substantially lower computational overhead.

Self-Supervised Training Data Generation. Several recent works explore how models can self-supervise the creation of training data to improve alignment. The original Constitutional AI technique (Bai et al., 2022b) also used critique and revision, but only for the purpose of reward modeling for subsequent reinforcement learning, and only for considering one principle at a time. Dromedary (Sun et al., 2023) simplifies this pipeline to only use supervised fine-tuning on examples generated with few-shot demonstrations of principles. SynPO (Dong et al., 2025) generates synthetic preference data through iterative self-improvement and uses this data to fine-tune models offline.

Reflect presents a novel pipeline that emphasizes inference-time constitutional alignment with in-context reasoning over conformance to multiple principles before and after initial generation in a way that simultaneously produces high-quality training data at no additional cost. This tight coupling between inference-time control and data generation enables a feedback loop in which alignment behavior deployed at test time directly produces the supervision required to improve future models. To our knowledge, Reflect is the first approach to unify inference-time alignment, multi-principle reasoning, and reusable supervision within a single framework.

Comparison to Other Self-Alignment Approaches. Across prior work, critique and revision have primarily been used either to improve general output quality or to generate training data for offline alignment. Reflect treats alignment as a test-time reasoning problem. It explicitly evaluates outputs against a multi-objective constitution, allowing for plug-and-play alignment to any constitution of principles, without requiring any other changes such as adapting few shot prompts. Additionally Reflect produces a dataset for supervised learning as a byproduct of normal use. This combination enables Reflect to be highly dynamic in adapting to new constitutional frameworks, address rare but severe alignment failures (even for state-of-the-art models) at inference time, and simultaneously generate training data to reduce such failures in future model deployments. 3. Methodology

In this section, we describe the Reflect technique in detail and describe our evaluation procedures.

3.1. Reflect

During Reflect, a single model 1) generates an initial constitution-conditioned base response, 2) evaluates the conformance of this base response against the constitution, and performs 3a) critique and 3b) revision of the base response. Algorithm 1 summarizes the Reflect process. Complete prompts used at each step are included in the Appendix. The prompts are not customized per constitution; Reflect is plug-and-play with respect to any desired constitution.

(1) Constitution-conditioned base response yCCBasey_{\texttt{CCBase}}. The LLM first generates a constitution-conditioned base response, yCCBasey_{\texttt{CCBase}}. The entire constitution is passed to the model, along with a simple system prompt instructing the LLM to incorporate all principles in its output (See Appendix G.4), and the user query. This is the starting point for the rest of the Reflect algorithm. An example of a constitution-conditioned base prompt is provided below.

(2) Self-evaluation. Before running a full cycle of critique and revision, the LLM first evaluates how well the base response conforms to each principle in the constitution by generating a Likert score between 1 and 5 for each principle.11 1 the exact prompt wording is available in Appendix G.2. If a principle’s score falls below a user-defined threshold, it is flagged, triggering the critique-and-revision step in which the model revisits the flagged principle. For all of our experimental results, we set a self-evaluation score of 33 as the threshold for revision. The self-evaluation step serves two key purposes. First, it decreases the computational overhead of Reflect by allowing the algorithm to skip the more costly critique-and-revision step when model responses are already well-aligned. Second, it helps to ensure that Reflect does not introduce new principle violations to already well-aligned responses. As noted by (Madaan et al., 2023), unnecessary revision can inadvertently degrade otherwise high-quality responses. A continued example of the self-evaluation prompt is shown below.

(3) Critique and Revision. For self-evaluation scores lower than the user-defined threshold, the model is prompted with πcritique-revise\pi_{\texttt{critique-revise}} (See Appendix G.3 for details) together with the constitution, user query, base response, and output of self-evaluation, to generate a critique and then a final revised response. The LLM is encouraged via a one-shot-prompt to follow a chain-of-thought style reasoning to first reason about the flagged principles, then perform a critique, and finally use the critique to arrive at a revised response. This order is crucial to ensure effectiveness and transparency, so that the critique is attended in-context by the causal LLM while generating the revision, rather than being a post-hoc rationalization of the final response.

Combining critique and revision within one prompt and reasoning process reduces computational overhead compared to separating these into multiple generations. The LLM can repeat Reflect steps 2) and 3) any number of times, stopping either after no principle falls below the threshold, or after a user-defined number of cycles. We found that for small to medium sized constitutions (5-12 principles), one round of critique and revision was often sufficient to see meaningful improvements. Thus, we use one full cycle of Reflect for all of our experimental results. A continued example of a critique and revision is provided below.

3.2. Evaluation

We evaluate Reflect on three model families, two datasets, and two unique constitutions of principles. We used a multi-objective approach to evaluate how well generations conformed to our constitutions. 22 2 A sample evaluation prompt is available in Appendix G.1.

Model Selection. We used three model families for our experiments. We used two advanced commercial models, GPT-4.1-Mini (Achiam et al., 2023) and Claude-Haiku-3.5 (Anthropic, 2024), and one smaller instruction-tuned model, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023) for our primary experimental Reflect results. We used the full-sized GPT-4.1 as the LLM judge for evaluation purposes.

Datasets. We tested Reflect against two red-teaming datasets: the 1) PKU-Safe-RLHF dataset consisting of single-turn prompts (Ji et al., 2025a) and the 2) Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset consisting of multi-turn conversation prompts (Bai et al., 2022a; Ganguli et al., 2022). We randomly sampled 500 prompts from each. For LLM self-finetuning using Reflect, (See §3.3) we used a subsample of 2000 prompts from the LMSYS-Chat-1M dataset (Zheng et al., 2023) to simulate real-world chatbot interactions.

Constitutions. We evaluated alignment under a diverse set of challenging principles, with a dedicated constitution defined for each dataset. For the PKU-Safe-RLHF dataset (Ji et al., 2025a) we use a twelve-principle constitution that we refer to as the ‘SafeRLHF constitution’. For the Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset (Bai et al., 2022a; Ganguli et al., 2022) we use a ten-principle constitution that we refer to as the ‘HH-RLHF constitution’. We specifically constructed these constitutions to contain principles that our evaluation models had not been parameter finetuned to follow. By using complex and at times orthogonal principles (for example, "Avoid anthropocentrism", "Include a historical parallel from a non-Western context"), we attempt to increase the task difficulty. This design serves as an intentionally challenging evaluation to capture real-world deployment scenarios in which models are expected to follow novel, context-specific, and value-laden constraints that may not be fully captured during training. Both constitutions are available in Appendix D.

Multi-objective evaluation. The use of LLM-as-a-judge has become increasingly common for evaluating language model outputs (Dubois et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023; Chan et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025). This approach is particularly useful when evaluating diverse attributes of model outputs at scale (Lin et al., 2023). We leverage a multi-objective evaluation approach similar to that used in (Lin et al., 2023) to evaluate how well Reflect outputs conform to our constitutions. For a given output, we prompt the full-sized GPT-4.1 (a stronger model than any models used for running Reflect) to generate a score for each principle between 1 (Completely violates principle) and 5 (Completely conforms to principle). We provide constitution-specific calibration examples in-context. Prompt details are available in the appendix. For some analyses, we recoded these scores into ‘violates principle’ (1-2), or ‘does not violate principle’ (3-5).

Importantly, our evaluation approach does not measure general human preference; rather, it specifically measures how well model responses conform to principles in a given constitution. This allows us to identify the impact of Reflect at the level of explicit principles, as well as the overall rate of conformance to a constitution for a set of generations.

LLM judge validation. To confirm that our LLM judge generated evaluation results are consistent with human judgments, we recruited 50 participants via Prolific and asked them to evaluate AI-generated responses. We showed participants prompts from both the HH-RLHF and SafeRLHF datasets, and asked them to evaluate model responses according to both of our constitutions. Our study was approved by our institutional review board (IRB) and all survey materials can be found in Appendix F.

We calculated the mean absolute difference between humans and the LLM judge on our 5-point Likert scale, as well as between each human. We also compared the rate of agreement on the recoded binary scale of ‘violates principle‘ (1-2) or ‘does not violate principle’ (3-5) between the human evaluators, and between human evaluators and the LLM judge. The results are shown in Table 2. The results indicate that, while principle conformance is inherently complex and subjective, our LLM-judge evaluations are reasonably consistent with human judgments.

3.3. Self-finetuning using Reflect

As a byproduct of inference-time usage, Reflect produces aligned responses that can be directly used as training data. The final revised outputs are suitable for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and the paired base and Reflect responses naturally form preference tuples for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We experiment with finetuning models using both training methods. Crucially, the training data is obtained at no additional data annotation or collection cost, enabling scalable alignment using data generated entirely from model interactions during deployment.

We supervised-finetuned33 3 Epochs = 3, batch size = 3, LR multiplier = 2 a GPT-4.1-Mini base model on 1,664 Reflect-revised responses from the LMSYS dataset (Zheng et al., 2023) to conform to the SafeRLHF constitution (shown in Figure 4). To improve performance when applying the Reflect pipeline on top of a self-finetuned model, we included our constitutional pre-conditioning prompt (see Appendix G.4) in 50% of the finetuning prompts. We DPO-finetuned44 4 Epochs = 2, batch size = 4, LR multiplier = 0.1, beta = 0.1 the same GPT-4.1-Mini base model using 1,364 Reflect-generated pairs from the LMSYS dataset.

4. Results

For all experimental results, we used constitution-conditioned base responses, (CCBase), from the same model as a baseline for comparison and the first step of the Reflect process (see Algorithm 1). We present our main results in Table 3.

4.1. Reflect Exhibits High Levels of Principle Conformance

As shown in Table 3, models undergoing Reflect achieve consistently high alignment scores, with averages ranging from 4.155 to 4.628 on a 5-point Likert scale. Notably, these strong performances are obtained despite the fact that the underlying LLMs have not been parameter fine-tuned to the target principles, underscoring the effectiveness of Reflect as an inference-time mechanism for scaling alignment. Compared to the constitution-conditioned base responses, Reflect yields consistent and substantial improvement across models and datasets. We conducted a paired bootstrap test to confirm that all improvements from Reflect are statistically significant at p=0.002p=0.002 (See Appendix §E). These results are further broken down by principle in Figure 2, revealing that the largest gains from Reflect typically arise from the most challenging principles. This highlights Reflect ’s ability to meaningfully strengthen alignment under the hardest constraints.

4.2. Reflect Targets Principle Violations

In cases where the constitution conditioned pre-generations are already highly conformant to a given constitution, Reflect may not significantly improve the average Likert evaluation scores of these generations. However, an analysis of the failure cases – where responses fail to conform to the constitution – shows that Reflect is effective at significantly reducing the rate at which principle violations occur, as seen in Table 3 and further broken down by principle in Figure 3. For example, consider GPT on Safe-RLHF. While Reflect improves the average score by less than 0.01 on the 5-point Likert scale, it reduces the rate of (relatively rare) violations (Likert scores of 1-2) by more than 50% compared to the CCBase responses. Compared to standard prompting techniques for model alignment, Reflect is able to self-correct in cases where initial generations fail to conform. This quality of Reflect specifically targets and reduces principle violations and has meaningful applications to domains such as safety, where infrequent failures may still present large threats.

4.3. Reflect Generates Fine-tuning Data

We evaluate the alignment of two finetuned GPT-4.1-Mini models (See §3.3) against a base GPT-4.1-Mini model without any additional constitutional prompting to replicate a realistic deployment scenario. Both self-finetuned models yielded improvements over the baseline model. The SFT-finetuned model achieved the strongest performance, approaching the average performance of the full Reflect pipeline (See Table 4).

4.4. Using Reflect on Complex Principles Maintains Factual Reasoning

We evaluate Reflect on factual reasoning benchmarks. We assessed Reflect using GPT-4.1-Mini and the SafeRLHF constitution on the GSM8k (Cobbe et al., 2021) and MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) benchmarks.

GSM8K comprises diverse grade-school mathematics word problems, designed to test LLM multi-step reasoning. MMLU is a multiple-choice benchmark spanning different disciplines and domains, including science, mathematics, law, and social science. Results are shown in Appendix Table 9. Importantly, aligning with Reflect represents a more challenging setting than standard inference in these factual problem-solving domains. The LLM must arrive at the correct answer and incorporate multiple principles within its reasoning trace. We compare this setting against a baseline that does not require conformance to any principles. We find that on GSM8K, Reflect does not impact performance at all. On MMLU, Reflect leads to a small decrease in accuracy of less than 2 points.

4.5. Reflect is Effective Across Different Model Sizes

We study the effectiveness of Reflect across model scales by performing a size ablation within the GPT-4.1 family, ranging from the largest model GPT-4.1, to GPT-4.1-Mini, to the smallest model of GPT-4.1-Nano. For each model, we compare the performance between the constitution-conditioned base response and the full Reflect procedure using the SafeRLHF dataset and constitution of 12 challenging principles. We present these results in Appendix Table 8. Across all model sizes, Reflect consistently improves principle conformance. The benefit of Reflect is the most pronounced for the smallest model, GPT-4.1-Nano. These results indicate that Reflect is robust to model scale, remaining effective even with smaller instruction-tuned models.

4.6. Reflect Has Low Overhead That Scales with Base-Model Alignment

To test the efficacy of our overhead-reduction strategies (See §3.1), we compare Reflect to a Constitutional Adaptation (Details in Appendix Reflect: Transparent Principle-Guided Reasoning for Constitutional Alignment at Scale) of another critique-and-revision module, Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023), which we hereafter refer to as CA_SelfRefine. The results are presented in Table 5. Across two constitutions, token overhead is significantly lower for Reflect while the principle violation rate remains comparable.

For both models token usage is significantly lower for the HHH constitution which consists of principles to which the base model is already aligned to (Achiam et al., 2023). We hypothesize that token overhead scales with the degree to which a base model is already aligned to a given constitution. During both Reflect and CA_SelfRefine many more initial responses required a revision to conform to SafeRLHF than to HHH. For example, the number of responses requiring at least 11 revision cycle in CA_SelfRefine increased by 6060% for SafeRLHF over HHH.

4.7. Reflect Does Not Unalign Models

We evaluated Reflect against 500 red-teaming prompts from the HH-RLHF dataset, using two different constitutions. First, we ran Reflect with a standard ‘honesty’, ‘helpfulness’, and ‘harmlessness’ constitution. We ran it again using ‘honesty’, ‘helpfulness’, and ‘harmfulness’. We show that ‘helpfulness’ scores remaining acceptably high even with a ’harmfulness’ constitution (See Table 6). A manual inspection of the generations from Reflect with the harmfulness principle showed that while the tone of the responses became more combative, it did not comply with the truly harmful requests of the red-teaming dataset. Additionally, the model refused to answer 12% of the user queries.

5. Discussion and Future Work

5.1. Applications to Pluralistic Alignment

Reflect presents a few advantages in the context of pluralistic alignment. As stakeholder values shift naturally over time, Reflect can easily be updated to ‘reflect’ new or changing values by simply modifying the constitution. Additionally, since Reflect dynamically aligns to arbitrary constitutions it can enable tailoring to small or under-served communities where collecting extensive training data or performing expensive finetuning procedures may be impractical or impossible. Lastly, as Reflect operates within the constitutional framework of alignment, it has some intrinsic level of transparency – the objectives that Reflect aligns to are specified in natural language and can be easily published, reviewed, and comprehended by relevant stakeholders. If desired, the full critique and revision reasoning could also be exposed to the user to provide even more insight into the model’s generations.

5.2. Reflect for Safety-critical Deployments

The in-context evaluation and critique elements of Reflect make it particularly well-suited for catching ‘tail-cases’: infrequent instances where models generate harmful or otherwise unaligned responses. We see in our experimental results that pre-conditioning alone is insufficient for generating consistently aligned model responses (See §4.2). In settings where consistent and accurate adherence to alignment principles is crucial, we believe Reflect can confer substantial improvements. In particular, we believe Reflect could be beneficial even when models are already generally well-aligned by identifying and rectifying rare misaligned response generations as they happen. Additionally, in real-world deployments where users have low or no restrictions on how they can interact with a model, adversarial attacks can often bypass alignment guardrails (Shen et al., 2024). We expect that the explicit reasoning Reflect undergoes, directly comparing its base generation to a constitution of principles, will make it more resistant to adversarial attacks of this kind. Future research should further investigate the ability of guided self-critique in an adversarial context.

5.3. Finetuning Models for Reflect

Our experimental results suggest that Reflect can be valuable for generating high-quality synthetic finetuning data for both DPO and SFT training. However, we also note that using these finetuned models within Reflect can actually reduce quality compared to using a generic instruction-tuned model for Reflect.

One possible explanation for this behavior is that the finetuned models learned to mimic the structure of aligned responses in a way that superficially aligns their generations. By approximating the structure of aligned responses, and mentioning principles explicitly by name, substantively unaligned responses may have gone undetected by the self-evaluation step of Reflect, and as a result avoided critique and revision altogether. Additionally, even when responses were flagged for critique and revision, it may be harder for a model to critique responses which are nearly aligned, but lack certain nuanced qualities necessary to fully conform to a principle. Future work should investigate finetuning procedures that 1) improve preconditioned generations while maintaining (or improving) the quality of the final Reflect outputs, and 2) train reasoning models to better perform critique and revision for use in Reflect.

Limitations

In this work, we only experimented with a very small subset of possible alignment principles. Future work should explore the principle space to identify principles that may be particularly challenging or adversarial against the Reflect algorithm. Additionally, Reflect may struggle to capture arbitrary ethical concerns that are not well-stated in the constitution. It should also be noted that Reflect does not guarantee perfect compliance. In fact it is technically possible for Reflect to introduce principle violations during critique and revision. This is, in part, due to the imperfection of the model self-evaluation step, which tends to report false positives (where the self-evaluation identifies principle violation where the LLM judge would not). In this vein, our LLM-judge is also an imperfect evaluator. For instance, it is likely that the LLM-judge favors responses which explicitly list each principle in a constitution, though this is not strictly necessary to conform to the principles. Finally, while Reflect offers increased transparency in comparison to black-box reward modeling, it is still possible that a reasoning trace generated by Reflect might be misleading or otherwise misrepresent the response generation process.

Abstract.
The constitutional framework of alignment aims to align large language models (LLMs) with value-laden principles written in natural language (such as to avoid using biased language). Prior work has focused on parameter fine-tuning techniques, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), to instill these principles. However, these approaches are computationally demanding, require careful engineering and tuning, and often require difficult-to-obtain human annotation data. We propose Reflect , an inference-time framework for constitutional alignment that does not require any training or data, providing a plug-and-play approach for aligning an instruction-tuned model to a set of principles. Reflect operates entirely in-context, combining a (i) constitution-conditioned base response with post-generation (ii) self-evaluation, (iii)(a) self-critique, and (iii)(b) final revision. Reflect ’s technique of explicit in-context reasoning over principles during post-generation outperforms standard few-shot prompting and provides transparent reasoning traces. Our results demonstrate that Reflect significantly improves LLM conformance to diverse and complex principles, including principles quite distinct from those emphasized in the model’s original parameter fine-tuning, without sacrificing factual reasoning. Reflect is particularly effective at reducing the rate of rare but significant violations of principles, thereby improving safety and robustness in the tail end of the distribution of generations. Finally, we show that Reflect naturally generates useful training data for traditional parameter fine-tuning techniques, allowing for efficient scaling and the reduction of inference-time computational overhead in long-term deployment scenarios.
Keywords:
alignment, in-context learning, constitutional AI, ethical AI, moral AI, principled AI
1. Introduction
As large language models (LLMs) display increasing capabilities ( Achiam et al., 2023 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Chowdhery et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , aligning these models with human values is critical for their safe and responsible deployment ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Gabriel, 2020 ; Christian, 2021 ; Askell et al., 2021 ; Ji et al., 2025b ) . The most common current alignment techniques, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and direct preference optimization (DPO), rely on fine-tuning a model’s parameters based on reward modeling from human or AI-generated annotations ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022b ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Ivison et al., 2024 ; Ethayarajh et al., 2024a ) . While valuable, such alignment techniques have a number of limitations. They are computationally demanding and often require difficult-to-obtain human annotation data ( Casper et al., 2023 ) . The need for lightweight inference-time techniques to adapt model behavior has led to the widespread use system prompts for adapting fine-tune modeled for particular use cases ( Lee et al., 2024b ; Neumann et al., 2025 ) . The algorithms generally require careful engineering and tuning and can suffer from challenges such as reward hacking ( Skalse et al., 2022 ) , learned deception ( Lang et al., 2024 ) , incentivizing sycophancy ( Sharma et al., 2024 ) , and conflicting and unstable human preferences ( Conitzer et al., 2024 ; Boerstler et al., 2024 ) . Standard model alignments have been found to exhibit bias towards particular cultures, demographics, and values ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Tao et al., 2024 ; Neumann et al., 2025 ; Schäfer et al., 2025 ; Taylor et al., 2025 ) .
Given these limitations, such parameter fine-tuning approaches with reward modeling are best suited for static alignment projects by well-resourced engineering teams before large-scale general deployments using fairly general principles such as helpfulness and harmlessness ( Askell et al., 2021 ; Bai et al., 2022a ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . There is a further need for alternative approaches to alignment that do not require any parameter fine-tuning or preference annotation data and that can be used to easily align to diverse cultures, values, and user groups ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Sorensen et al., 2024 ; Tao et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2024b ; Kirk et al., 2024 ; Ramesh et al., 2024 ; Davani et al., 2024 ; Schäfer et al., 2025 ) . Even within a given population, such techniques may still be helpful to align to diverse deployment contexts and their germane values. For example, the relevant values and alignment principles may differ based on whether an LLM is deployed for use in hospitals, mental health, education, entertainment, or software development. Such contextual diversity can be accommodated within the constitutional alignment framework ( Bai et al., 2022b ; Huang et al., 2024b ; Fränken et al., 2024b ; Findeis et al., 2024 ; Kyrychenko et al., 2025 ) in which the relevant principles are explicitly and transparently stated in natural language text (for example, “Do not employ stereotypes based on race”). We work within this constitutional alignment framework and primarily evaluate conformance to the stated principles.
1.1. Introducing Reflect
In this work, we propose Reflect , an inference-time technique to dynamically align an LLM to a constitution of value-laden principles written in natural language. Reflect uses in-context reasoning in multiple stages: (i) constitutional pre-conditioning for initial generation, (ii) constitutional self-evaluation post-generation, (iii)(a) self-critique, and (iii)(b) final revision. A simplified example of the Reflect process is diagrammed in Figure 1 .
Figure 1. Given an input query and a constitution of principles, Reflect first generates a constitution-conditioned base response. It then self-evaluates the response before performing critique and revision to generate the final, improved response.
Unique from most alignment techniques, Reflect explicitly reasons in natural language over conformance or violation of multiple principles without relying on a numerical reward model. Reflect requires no training data, only a specification of principles in natural language. Furthermore, unlike most prompt-engineering approaches that focus only on the initial prompt engineering ( Wei et al., 2022 ; Lin et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2024b ; Khan et al., 2025 ) , Reflect also uses post-generation principled self-critique and revision. Post-generation inference-time compute techniques for self-correction have previously been studied for mathematical reasoning, coding, and factual question-answering, ( Madaan et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024a ) . We show that such techniques can be applied to substantially improve model alignment to a constitution of principles. The effectiveness of post-generation principled self-critique and revision highlights a key insight of Reflect : instruction-tuned LLMs are better at identifying when their generations violate principles than they are at generating principle-aligned responses in the first place, likely due to the capabilities of in-context learning under causal attention in the Transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Brown et al., 2020 ) .
Expanding on these observations, we show that Reflect substantially improves constitutional alignment even for advanced models like GPT-4 ( Achiam et al., 2023 ) , Claude 3 ( Anthropic, 2024 ) , and Mistral ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) . We focus on a multi-objective evaluation of conformance to the stated principles, rather than general benchmarks of human preference ( Dubois et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024a ; Li et al., 2024b ) and find that Reflect is particularly effective at substantially reducing the rate of serious principle violations. Such violations are rare and in the tail of the distribution of generations – they may not significantly affect scores on standard benchmarks. However, from a safety, risk, and compliance perspective, mitigating such violations of alignment principles is nonetheless crucial.
Finally, we show that Reflect creates its own synthetic training dataset (for traditional parameter fine-tuning) as a byproduct of usage. Specifically, on a given prompt Reflect generates a baseline response and a revised response after principled self-critique and revision. We show that one can fine-tune a model using these base and revised generations. This creates a natural feedback loop between inference-time alignment and offline fine-tuning, where alignment behavior deployed at test time directly produces the data needed to improve future models.
Reflect addresses three crucial aspects of responsible AI: diversity, transparency, and safety. LLM deployments are diverse with respect to users, values, cultures, and contexts ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Kirk et al., 2024 ; Tao et al., 2024 ; Davani et al., 2024 ; Sorensen et al., 2024 ; Khan et al., 2025 ; Fazelpour and Fleisher, 2025 ; Schäfer et al., 2025 ; Taylor et al., 2025 ) . As an inference-time in-context reasoning technique requiring only principles, not parameter fine-tuning or training data, Reflect enables pluralistic alignment for specific deployment contexts that would otherwise be impractical. Many traditional alignment techniques (even many constitutional approaches) often rely on black-box reward modeling ( Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022a ; Bai et al., 2022b ) or directly optimize against a human annotation dataset ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Ethayarajh et al., 2024b ) . By contrast, Reflect increases transparency through explicit in-context reasoning in natural language about whether outputs conform to stated principles. Finally, rather than optimizing for and evaluating against average human preference between responses ( Dubois et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024b ) we emphasize safety as conformance to stated principles and conduct tail analysis for the rate of rare but significant violations.
1.2. Contributions and Summary of Findings
(1)
We define Reflect in Section 3 , an inference-time alignment technique to align LLM generations to a constitution of principles without any additional human annotated data or parameter fine-tuning.
(2)
Our main findings in Section 4 show that Reflect is highly effective at enforcing conformance across prompts, constitutions, and models (notably, models that have not been fine-tuned on the constitutions). Post-generation in-context reasoning consistently improves performance over pre-generation prompting alone.
(3)
While Reflect is a purely in-context reasoning technique, we show that running Reflect naturally generates valuable alignment training data if subsequent parameter fine-tuning is desired for a long-term deployment. Specifically, in Section 4.3 we show that the prompts, base generations, and final revisions of Reflect , gathered naturally during inference, can be used to parameter fine-tune a model so as to improve the model’s alignment.
(4)
Reflect does not significantly affect factual reasoning on GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) and MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) benchmarks. (Section 4.4 )
(5)
We find that Reflect is effective across different model sizes. (Section 4.5 )
(6)
We measure the computational overhead of Reflect , which achieves similar performance while using 2-5 times fewer tokens compared to straightforward adaptations of alternative self-correction techniques ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) . The overhead is lower when a model is already well aligned to a given constitution. (Section 4.6 )
(7)
Finally, we find that Reflect is generally ineffective at “un-aligning” or “jailbreaking” a model. (Section 4.7 )
2. Related Work
Alignment and Pluralism. Alignment ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Gabriel, 2020 ; Christian, 2021 ; Askell et al., 2021 ; Ji et al., 2025b ) is the critical challenge of ensuring that AI models conform to human expectations and values. Alignment involves the normative question of identifying the relevant values ( Klingefjord et al., 2024 ; Findeis et al., 2024 ; Kirk et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024b ; Gabriel and Keeling, 2025 ) , but also the sociotechnical question of how to engineer models to conform to given values. Reflect focuses on the latter and largely technical question. It takes principles as input, and this paper does not adopt a position on the correct principles. However, as a technique, Reflect is motivated by and contributes to alignment research emphasizing metaprinciples of transparency and pluralism. Regarding transparency, Reflect adopts a constitutional framework in which principles are stated explicitly in natural language ( Bai et al., 2022b ; Huang et al., 2024b ; Fränken et al., 2024a ; Findeis et al., 2024 ) . Regarding pluralism ( Sorensen et al., 2024 ; Khan et al., 2025 ) , prior work has shown that there are substantive disagreements about appropriate values for alignment ( Huang et al., 2024b ; Kirk et al., 2024 ; Fazelpour and Fleisher, 2025 ) and that many current models, in fact, exhibit cultural biases regarding alignment values ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Tao et al., 2024 ; Davani et al., 2024 ; Neumann et al., 2025 ; Schäfer et al., 2025 ; Taylor et al., 2025 ) . Reflect is designed to be easy to use without parameter fine-tuning or extensive data collection, enabling more dynamic and fine-grained control over the model alignment values used across different deployment contexts.
Finetuning-based Alignment.
Many alignment techniques directly fine-tune model parameters. For example, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022a ) uses human preference annotations to train a reward model for use in proximal policy optimization (PPO) ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) to fine-tune a language model. Subsequent work simplifies training by showing how to directly optimize for the margin between preferred and dispreferred responses given human preference data without intermediate reward modeling, including direct preference optimization (DPO) ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) and its generalizations Ψ \Psi PO ( Azar et al., 2024 ) and GPO ( Tang et al., 2024 ) . Other work introduces more sophisticated utility modeling such as prospect theoretic optimization (KTO) ( Ethayarajh et al., 2024b ) . While these works rely on access to human-annotated preference data, alternative fine-tuning techniques utilize reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) ( Bai et al., 2022b ; Lee et al., 2024a ) , supervised fine-tuning with AI-generated examples ( Sun et al., 2023 ) , conditional mutual information maximization ( Fränken et al., 2024a ) , or mixture-of-agents data-generation ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . In contrast to all of these approaches, Reflect involves no training of model parameters and relies entirely on inference-time reasoning conducted in-context.
Inference-time Reasoning and Alignment.
Techniques to improve model performance without parameter fine-tuning generally rely on in-context reasoning or sequence decoding. Pre-generation approaches focus on initial prompting: chain-of-thought (CoT) structures and few-shot examples ( Wei et al., 2022 ) while other techniques rely on the system prompt ( Lin et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2024b ) . With Reflect , we show that post-generation self-evaluation, critique, and revision (all of which condition on the base generation of the model) substantially improves constitutional conformance.
Techniques such as repeated sampling ( Brown et al., 2024 ) and guided decoding ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) demonstrate that one can improve alignment without adjusting prompting. Reflect differs from these approaches by treating inference-time alignment as an explicit reasoning process rather than a decoding constraint. Instead of implicitly optimizing toward preferences, Reflect evaluates generated responses against a set of natural-language principles and performs targeted revision through self-critique. This enables alignment to multiple, potentially conflicting objectives specified at runtime, and supports dynamic adaptation to principles that may be rare, domain-specific, or absent from standard alignment datasets.
Prior work finds that post-generation iterative self-refinement can be effective at improving task-specific performance including math reasoning, sentiment reversal, and dialogue generation ( Madaan et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) , and at reducing hallucinations ( Gao et al., 2023 ) , though other work has questioned the effectiveness of such self-correction ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Kamoi et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024c ) . These works overwhelmingly focus on mathematical or factual reasoning. We extend these investigations to constitutional alignment and systematically evaluate diverse constitutions for conformance to principles on average and in the tail. Our results highlight a novel advantage for post-generation in-context reasoning in the context of safety in constitutional alignment. Compared to the findings in ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) , we show that Reflect generalizes to diverse value-laden principles unlike those used for parameter fine-tuning, generates its own valuable training data for subsequent fine-tuning, is effective even at small model sizes, and has substantially lower computational overhead.
Self-Supervised Training Data Generation.
Several recent works explore how models can self-supervise the creation of training data to improve alignment. The original Constitutional AI technique ( Bai et al., 2022b ) also used critique and revision, but only for the purpose of reward modeling for subsequent reinforcement learning, and only for considering one principle at a time. Dromedary ( Sun et al., 2023 ) simplifies this pipeline to only use supervised fine-tuning on examples generated with few-shot demonstrations of principles. SynPO ( Dong et al., 2025 ) generates synthetic preference data through iterative self-improvement and uses this data to fine-tune models offline.
Reflect presents a novel pipeline that emphasizes inference-time constitutional alignment with in-context reasoning over conformance to multiple principles before and after initial generation in a way that simultaneously produces high-quality training data at no additional cost.
This tight coupling between inference-time control and data generation enables a feedback loop in which alignment behavior deployed at test time directly produces the supervision required to improve future models. To our knowledge, Reflect is the first approach to unify inference-time alignment, multi-principle reasoning, and reusable supervision within a single framework.
Comparison to Other Self-Alignment Approaches. Across prior work, critique and revision have primarily been used either to improve general output quality or to generate training data for offline alignment. Reflect treats alignment as a test-time reasoning problem. It explicitly evaluates outputs against a multi-objective constitution, allowing for plug-and-play alignment to any constitution of principles, without requiring any other changes such as adapting few shot prompts. Additionally Reflect produces a dataset for supervised learning as a byproduct of normal use. This combination enables Reflect to be highly dynamic in adapting to new constitutional frameworks, address rare but severe alignment failures (even for state-of-the-art models) at inference time, and simultaneously generate training data to reduce such failures in future model deployments. (3) Critique and Revision. For self-evaluation scores lower than the user-defined threshold, the model is prompted with π critique-revise \pi_{\texttt{critique-revise}} (See Appendix G.3 for details) together with the constitution, user query, base response, and output of self-evaluation, to generate a critique and then a final revised response. The LLM is encouraged via a one-shot-prompt to follow a chain-of-thought style reasoning to first reason about the flagged principles, then perform a critique, and finally use the critique to arrive at a revised response. This order is crucial to ensure effectiveness and transparency, so that the critique is attended in-context by the causal LLM while generating the revision, rather than being a post-hoc rationalization of the final response.
Combining critique and revision within one prompt and reasoning process reduces computational overhead compared to separating these into multiple generations. The LLM can repeat Reflect steps 2) and 3) any number of times, stopping either after no principle falls below the threshold, or after a user-defined number of cycles. We found that for small to medium sized constitutions (5-12 principles), one round of critique and revision was often sufficient to see meaningful improvements. 3.2. Evaluation
We evaluate Reflect on three model families, two datasets, and two unique constitutions of principles. We used a multi-objective approach to evaluate how well generations conformed to our constitutions. 2 2
2
A sample evaluation prompt is available in Appendix G.1 .
Model Selection.
We used three model families for our experiments. We used two advanced commercial models, GPT-4.1-Mini ( Achiam et al., 2023 ) and Claude-Haiku-3.5 ( Anthropic, 2024 ) , and one smaller instruction-tuned model, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) for our primary experimental Reflect results. We used the full-sized GPT-4.1 as the LLM judge for evaluation purposes.
Datasets.
We tested Reflect against two red-teaming datasets: the 1) PKU-Safe-RLHF dataset consisting of single-turn prompts ( Ji et al., 2025a ) and the 2) Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset consisting of multi-turn conversation prompts ( Bai et al., 2022a ; Ganguli et al., 2022 ) . We randomly sampled 500 prompts from each. For LLM self-finetuning using Reflect , (See § 3.3 ) we used a subsample of 2000 prompts from the LMSYS-Chat-1M dataset ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) to simulate real-world chatbot interactions.
Constitutions.
We evaluated alignment under a diverse set of challenging principles, with a dedicated constitution defined for each dataset. For the PKU-Safe-RLHF dataset ( Ji et al., 2025a ) we use a twelve-principle constitution that we refer to as the ‘SafeRLHF constitution’. For the Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset ( Bai et al., 2022a ; Ganguli et al., 2022 ) we use a ten-principle constitution that we refer to as the ‘HH-RLHF constitution’. We specifically constructed these constitutions to contain principles that our evaluation models had not been parameter finetuned to follow. By using complex and at times orthogonal principles (for example, "Avoid anthropocentrism", "Include a historical parallel from a non-Western context"), we attempt to increase the task difficulty. This design serves as an intentionally challenging evaluation to capture real-world deployment scenarios in which models are expected to follow novel, context-specific, and value-laden constraints that may not be fully captured during training. Both constitutions are available in Appendix D .
Multi-objective evaluation.
The use of LLM-as-a-judge has become increasingly common for evaluating language model outputs ( Dubois et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Chan et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . This approach is particularly useful when evaluating diverse attributes of model outputs at scale ( Lin et al., 2023 ) . We leverage a multi-objective evaluation approach similar to that used in ( Lin et al., 2023 ) to evaluate how well Reflect outputs conform to our constitutions. For a given output, we prompt the full-sized GPT-4.1 (a stronger model than any models used for running Reflect ) to generate a score for each principle between 1 (Completely violates principle) and 5 (Completely conforms to principle). We provide constitution-specific calibration examples in-context. Prompt details are available in the appendix. For some analyses, we recoded these scores into ‘violates principle’ (1-2), or ‘does not violate principle’ (3-5).
Importantly, our evaluation approach does not measure general human preference; rather, it specifically measures how well model responses conform to principles in a given constitution. This allows us to identify the impact of Reflect at the level of explicit principles, as well as the overall rate of conformance to a constitution for a set of generations.
LLM judge validation.
To confirm that our LLM judge generated evaluation results are consistent with human judgments, we recruited 50 participants via Prolific and asked them to evaluate AI-generated responses. We showed participants prompts from both the HH-RLHF and SafeRLHF datasets, and asked them to evaluate model responses according to both of our constitutions. Our study was approved by our institutional review board (IRB) and all survey materials can be found in Appendix F .
We calculated the mean absolute difference between humans and the LLM judge on our 5-point Likert scale, as well as between each human. We also compared the rate of agreement on the recoded binary scale of ‘violates principle‘ (1-2) or ‘does not violate principle’ (3-5) between the human evaluators, and between human evaluators and the LLM judge. The results are shown in Table 2 . The results indicate that, while principle conformance is inherently complex and subjective, our LLM-judge evaluations are reasonably consistent with human judgments.

4.1. Reflect Exhibits High Levels of Principle Conformance
As shown in Table 3 , models undergoing Reflect achieve consistently high alignment scores, with averages ranging from 4.155 to 4.628 on a 5-point Likert scale. Notably, these strong performances are obtained despite the fact that the underlying LLMs have not been parameter fine-tuned to the target principles, underscoring the effectiveness of Reflect as an inference-time mechanism for scaling alignment. Compared to the constitution-conditioned base responses, Reflect yields consistent and substantial improvement across models and datasets. We conducted a paired bootstrap test to confirm that all improvements from Reflect are statistically significant at p = 0.002 p=0.002 (See Appendix § E ). These results are further broken down by principle in Figure 2 , revealing that the largest gains from Reflect typically arise from the most challenging principles. This highlights Reflect ’s ability to meaningfully strengthen alignment under the hardest constraints.
4.2. Reflect Targets Principle Violations
In cases where the constitution conditioned pre-generations are already highly conformant to a given constitution, Reflect may not significantly improve the average Likert evaluation scores of these generations. However, an analysis of the failure cases – where responses fail to conform to the constitution – shows that Reflect is effective at significantly reducing the rate at which principle violations occur, as seen in Table 3 and further broken down by principle in Figure 3 . For example, consider GPT on Safe-RLHF. While Reflect improves the average score by less than 0.01 on the 5-point Likert scale, it reduces the rate of (relatively rare) violations (Likert scores of 1-2) by more than 50% compared to the CCBase responses. Compared to standard prompting techniques for model alignment, Reflect is able to self-correct in cases where initial generations fail to conform. This quality of Reflect specifically targets and reduces principle violations and has meaningful applications to domains such as safety, where infrequent failures may still present large threats.

4.4. Using Reflect on Complex Principles Maintains Factual Reasoning
We evaluate Reflect on factual reasoning benchmarks. We assessed Reflect using GPT-4.1-Mini and the SafeRLHF constitution on the GSM8k ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) and MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) benchmarks.
GSM8K comprises diverse grade-school mathematics word problems, designed to test LLM multi-step reasoning. MMLU is a multiple-choice benchmark spanning different disciplines and domains, including science, mathematics, law, and social science. Results are shown in Appendix Table 9 . Importantly, aligning with Reflect represents a more challenging setting than standard inference in these factual problem-solving domains. The LLM must arrive at the correct answer and incorporate multiple principles within its reasoning trace. We compare this setting against a baseline that does not require conformance to any principles. We find that on GSM8K, Reflect does not impact performance at all. On MMLU, Reflect leads to a small decrease in accuracy of less than 2 points.

For each model, we compare the performance between the constitution-conditioned base response and the full Reflect procedure using the SafeRLHF dataset and constitution of 12 challenging principles. 5. Discussion and Future Work
5.1. Applications to Pluralistic Alignment
Reflect presents a few advantages in the context of pluralistic alignment. As stakeholder values shift naturally over time, Reflect can easily be updated to ‘reflect’ new or changing values by simply modifying the constitution. Additionally, since Reflect dynamically aligns to arbitrary constitutions it can enable tailoring to small or under-served communities where collecting extensive training data or performing expensive finetuning procedures may be impractical or impossible. Lastly, as Reflect operates within the constitutional framework of alignment, it has some intrinsic level of transparency – the objectives that Reflect aligns to are specified in natural language and can be easily published, reviewed, and comprehended by relevant stakeholders. If desired, the full critique and revision reasoning could also be exposed to the user to provide even more insight into the model’s generations.
5.2. Reflect for Safety-critical Deployments
The in-context evaluation and critique elements of Reflect make it particularly well-suited for catching ‘tail-cases’: infrequent instances where models generate harmful or otherwise unaligned responses. We see in our experimental results that pre-conditioning alone is insufficient for generating consistently aligned model responses (See § 4.2 ). In settings where consistent and accurate adherence to alignment principles is crucial, we believe Reflect can confer substantial improvements. In particular, we believe Reflect could be beneficial even when models are already generally well-aligned by identifying and rectifying rare misaligned response generations as they happen. Additionally, in real-world deployments where users have low or no restrictions on how they can interact with a model, adversarial attacks can often bypass alignment guardrails ( Shen et al., 2024 ) . We expect that the explicit reasoning Reflect undergoes, directly comparing its base generation to a constitution of principles, will make it more resistant to adversarial attacks of this kind. Future research should further investigate the ability of guided self-critique in an adversarial context.
5.3. Finetuning Models for Reflect
Our experimental results suggest that Reflect can be valuable for generating high-quality synthetic finetuning data for both DPO and SFT training. However, we also note that using these finetuned models within Reflect can actually reduce quality compared to using a generic instruction-tuned model for Reflect .
One possible explanation for this behavior is that the finetuned models learned to mimic the structure of aligned responses in a way that superficially aligns their generations. By approximating the structure of aligned responses, and mentioning principles explicitly by name, substantively unaligned responses may have gone undetected by the self-evaluation step of Reflect , and as a result avoided critique and revision altogether. Additionally, even when responses were flagged for critique and revision, it may be harder for a model to critique responses which are nearly aligned, but lack certain nuanced qualities necessary to fully conform to a principle. Future work should investigate finetuning procedures that 1) improve preconditioned generations while maintaining (or improving) the quality of the final Reflect outputs, and 2) train reasoning models to better perform critique and revision for use in Reflect .
Limitations
In this work, we only experimented with a very small subset of possible alignment principles. Future work should explore the principle space to identify principles that may be particularly challenging or adversarial against the Reflect algorithm. Additionally, Reflect may struggle to capture arbitrary ethical concerns that are not well-stated in the constitution. It should also be noted that Reflect does not guarantee perfect compliance. In fact it is technically possible for Reflect to introduce principle violations during critique and revision. This is, in part, due to the imperfection of the model self-evaluation step, which tends to report false positives (where the self-evaluation identifies principle violation where the LLM judge would not). In this vein, our LLM-judge is also an imperfect evaluator. For instance, it is likely that the LLM-judge favors responses which explicitly list each principle in a constitution, though this is not strictly necessary to conform to the principles.
Finally, while Reflect offers increased transparency in comparison to black-box reward modeling, it is still possible that a reasoning trace generated by Reflect might be misleading or otherwise misrepresent the response generation process.
